caep.off: CAEP is turned off (caep.enabled). The eight event types are dropped from events_supported, so a stream asking for one gets it back missing from events_delivered — which is the only notice SSF gives, and is exactly the case a receiver ought to be tested against. SSF itself is unaffected.
caep.intro1: CAEP (OpenID Continuous Access Evaluation Profile 1.0, final 2 September 2025) is the enterprise session vocabulary spoken over
caep.intro2: . SSF is the PIPE and defines two events of its own, both about the pipe; these eight are about a session, and the sentence they carry is this session is no longer trustworthy. RISC says this account is no longer trustworthy, which is a different sentence and the whole reason there are two profiles.
caep.autoWarn: This is the one place in this service where an endpoint is not what starts the work. With caep.autoEmit on, a sign-in emits session-established, an authorization request answered from a session that already existed emits session-presented, and a sign-out emits session-revoked — on every stream that asked for the type and whose subjects cover that session, with nobody having typed anything. Every other family here answers a request. Turning it off restores the older and equally honest behaviour: every Security Event Token this service sends was asked for.
caep.emitNote: Every one of the eight is also sent on its own when the act it describes happens here (a device's compliance since #164); this form sends one on demand, with the payload you choose. The subject is composed from the session you pick: SSF's complex subject, naming the person AND the session, because the person is not revoked and one session of theirs is. Leave the payload empty for a conforming specimen of the type.
caep.emittingAbout: Emitting about {who}’s session {id}{hasProtocol, select, yes {, established over {protocol}} other {}}. The subject below is composed from it.
caep.noLive1: No live session has the id {id}. It may have been signed out since this link was made — a revoked row stays on
caep.noLive2: and is not offered here. Search again above.
caep.pickNote: Pick a session above and the form below will emit about it. Until one is picked there is nothing to be about: a CAEP event names a SESSION, and this form will not compose a subject out of an identifier nobody chose.
caep.noLiveSessions: There are no LIVE sessions to emit about. A CAEP event is ABOUT a session — the subject names one — so sign somebody in first. Anything that starts a session will do, and that is the point rather than a convenience: CAEP is a vocabulary about SESSIONS and not about OAuth, so an OIDC flow, a SAML 2.0 or SAML 1.1 sign-in, WS-Federation and SPNEGO all reach the same funnel here and all produce a row.
caep.catalogueNote: Each row's members are the specification's own, with the four CAEP section 2 gives EVERY event beneath them: event_timestamp, initiating_entity, reason_admin and reason_user. All four are OPTIONAL, which surprises people about the first — a receiver deciding whether to end a session wants it more than anything else in the payload, and a conforming transmitter need not send one. caep.omitEventTimestamp produces that event on purpose.
chooser.sessionPlaceholder: part of a username, a subject or a session id
chooser.noLiveMatch1: No live session belongs to anybody matching that. This list holds the sessions this service still considers OPEN — a revoked one stays on
chooser.noLiveMatch2: as evidence and is deliberately not offered here, because the state machine refuses a session-presented about a session that has ended.
chooser.accountPlaceholder: part of a username, a subject or an email address
chooser.noAccountMatch: No tracked account matches that. This register holds one row per account this service has been told anything about — including ones that no longer exist — and it will be empty until the directory changes or somebody emits an event by hand. You can type an account name into the form below regardless: a RISC event names a person, and this service can name any person at all.
risc.subjectMust: Its subject must be {formats}, and it carries the OLD value.
risc.noMembers: No payload members at all. The subject carries the entire message.
risc.off: RISC is turned off (risc.enabled). The fourteen event types are dropped from events_supported, so a stream asking for one gets it back missing from events_delivered — which is the only notice SSF gives. SSF and CAEP are unaffected.
risc.intro1: RISC (OpenID RISC Profile Specification 1.0, published 29 August 2025 and final on 2 September 2025) is the account vocabulary spoken over
risc.intro2: , and the second of the two.
risc.intro3: says this session is no longer trustworthy; RISC says this account is no longer trustworthy. Those are two different sentences and the second is the larger by orders of magnitude — a revoked session is one sign-in at one relying party, and a purged account is every session that person has anywhere, for ever. CAEP is aimed WITHIN an enterprise and RISC ACROSS providers: its origin is a consumer provider noticing an account has been taken over and telling every site that account signs in to.
risc.subjectIsMessage: Eleven of the fourteen carry no payload members at all, so the subject IS the message. account-purged says nothing but its own type and who it is about — which means a subject naming the wrong person is not a partly wrong event, it is a completely wrong one with nothing else in it to notice by. risc.subjectFormat below is therefore the most consequential setting on this page.
risc.directory1: This service emits RISC events when its own DIRECTORY changes, which is a different observer from CAEP's. With risc.autoEmit on, a person deleted emits account-purged, active going false or true emits account-disabled or account-enabled, and a changed mail address or telephone number emits identifier-changed. Those acts reach this directory over
risc.directory3: and from the console alike, because the observer sits on the WRITE rather than on any one door.
risc.activeNote: Setting active to false DISABLES the account since 2026-09-17 — it read "deactivates nobody" until then. It writes the password-policy lock pwdAccountLockedTime, every door refuses that person while it is set, and everything they hold is ended at once. The RISC event is unchanged and is what it always was: a transmitter reports and a receiver decides — what changed is that this service now acts on it too.
risc.googleWarn: risc.googleSubjectType is on, so every RISC subject leaving here spells its discriminator subject_type rather than format. That is RISC section 3.1's own compatibility note about a production transmitter in the field: the specification says new services MUST NOT use the name and then tells relying parties they need code to work around it anyway. This is how a receiver finds out whether it has that code. CAEP and SSF events are untouched.
risc.emitNote: Ten of the fourteen describe things nothing here does — no breach corpus is searched by this service and no recovery flow runs in it — so this form is the only way they are ever produced. Four of those ten CHANGE REAL STATE when they go: RISC section 2.8 defines each opt-out event as the account is in this state rather than as a report that it moved, so emitting one here IS the transition. The subject is composed from the account you pick, in the format risc.subjectFormat names — except for the two identifier events, which use an email address regardless, because for those two the identifier is the message.
risc.emittingAbout: Emitting about {who} — {subject}. Its lifecycle is {lifecycle} and its opt-out state is {optOut}.
risc.pickNote: Pick an account above, or type one below. An account this service has never held is accepted, which is the opposite of what the CAEP form does with an unknown session and is the specification's difference rather than an inconsistency: a session identifier this service never minted is one it can compose no subject from, and an account is a person. RISC is aimed ACROSS providers, so the account a receiver is warned about is usually one it has never seen.
risc.reasonNote: The two reason fields reach the wire for ONE of the fourteen types. RISC gives reason_admin, reason_user and event_timestamp to credential-compromise and to nothing else — where CAEP gives four claims to all eight of its own — so on any other type they are composed and dropped by the catalogue rather than sent as members the specification does not define.
risc.catalogueNote: Only one of the fourteen has a required member — credential-compromise's credential_type, which RISC defines BY REFERENCE to CAEP's credential-change, so the two lists are the same list rather than two alike ones. Eleven have no members at all. And one member name in the whole of Shared Signals uses a HYPHEN: identifier-changed's new-value, where everything else in all three vocabularies is snake_case, so new_value typed from habit produces an event that delivers and says nothing.
sessions.otherNames: {n} session(s) are tracked under other names.
noneTracked: None is tracked at all yet.
sessions.none: No sessions are tracked. Sign somebody in — an OIDC flow, a SAML 2.0 sign-in, WS-Federation — and a row appears here whether or not any stream is agreed, which is what makes “nothing arrived” traceable to “nobody asked”.
sessions.noStreams: No streams. Nothing this service says about a session has anywhere to go, and every row above will show a count of zero however many people sign in.
sessions.caepOff: CAEP is turned off (caep.enabled), so nothing new is being recorded here. What is below is what was recorded before it was turned off.
sessions.autoOff1: Automatic emission is off (caep.autoEmit). Sessions still appear here and their state still follows what really happens, and nothing goes out unless somebody emits it from
sessions.autoOff2: . That is this service's older behaviour: every Security Event Token it sends was asked for.
sessions.intro1: One row per session this service has held, including sessions it no longer holds. That is deliberate and it is the whole reason this page exists: the session store forgets a session the moment it is signed out, so a row whose state is revoked is the only remaining evidence that it existed and was revoked. The counts are per event type and they never forget; WHICH events those were is
sessions.intro2: , which is a different question and is a click away from every identifier below.
sessions.omitWarn: caep.omitEventTimestamp is on, so every event leaving here carries NO event_timestamp. That is perfectly conforming — CAEP section 2 makes it optional — and it is what a receiver that assumes one falls over on.
sessions.heading: Sessions
sessions.drillNote: Every identifier in the first column opens that session on its own page — what has actually been sent about it, in order, with what the register noticed as each one was applied. That was a card per session under this table until 2026-09-04, which meant this table was off the top of the screen the moment more than a handful of people had signed in.
sessions.searchLabel: Narrow to a person or a session
sessions.searchPlaceholder: a username, a subject or a session id
sessions.searchWhat: It matches the username, the sub, the session identifier, the SSF subject as a receiver was sent it, and the protocol the session was started through — because a reader arrives holding exactly one of those and does not know which column it will be in. It narrows this table only; the streams below it are about the transmitter rather than about anybody.
sessions.perPage: Only the sessions table is paged. The streams under it are one row per stream agreed with this transmitter, which is a number somebody configured rather than one that grows by itself.
sessions.whereHeading: Where a CAEP event could go
sessions.zeroNote: A session with a count of zero almost always means no stream asked for that type rather than anything being wrong. SSF has no refusal for an event type a transmitter will not deliver — its absence from events_delivered is the only notice a receiver gets — so this table is where that shows up.
sessions.perApp1: What this transmitter has said to each receiver, across every session. The table above this one is per STREAM and the one above that is per SESSION; this is the third question, and it is the one somebody actually arrives with once more than one receiver exists: is the application I am testing getting anything, and what. The counts are per event type and they never forget — they are counted when the Security Event Token is built and queued, which is when this service has SAID something, so a poll stream nobody has polled yet still shows what is waiting for it.
sessions.perApp2: An application with no stream is a row rather than an omission, and it is the commonest state a receiver under test is in: declared here with the Shared Signals box ticked, nothing agreed yet. Every count is zero and the Streams column says so, which is the first thing to check when nothing arrives. A row whose Takes column says none of CAEP's eight is the second: SSF has no refusal for a type a transmitter will not deliver, so the type's absence from events_delivered is the only notice a receiver ever gets.
sessions.perApp3: The identifier is what the receiver authenticated as when it created the stream, and aud is what it asked its Security Event Tokens to be addressed to. They are different fields and this is the only place both are shown: aud is REQUIRED on a stream and is deliberately never defaulted to the caller, because an audience this service invented would be one the receiver never learns it has to check for. Where they agree the column says so rather than repeating the name. A row named (no application) is the collected total for streams agreed while ssf.authRequired was off — there was no principal to record, and those events are real.
receiverPlaceholder: an application name, an identifier or an aud
sessions.receiverWhat: It matches the application name, the identifier it authenticated as, and the aud on its streams — the three strings a reader arrives holding, which are routinely different. It does NOT match the event types: a receiver that takes none of the eight is exactly the row somebody is looking for when they ask why nothing arrived.
apps.otherNames: {n} receiver(s) are known under other names.
apps.noneKnown: None is known at all yet.
apps.none1: No application here supports Shared Signals yet. An entry appears the moment a receiver creates a stream at /ssf/stream, and one can be declared ahead of that by ticking Shared Signals on
apps.noneRisc: No application here supports Shared Signals yet. An entry appears the moment a receiver creates a stream at /ssf/stream.
apps.matchPaged: , of which rows {first}–{last} are on this page ({page} of {pages})
apps.matchTail: . Busiest first. Delivered / failed is the PIPE — how many Security Event Tokens left this service and how many could not be handed over — and it is a different number from the total beside it, which is what was SAID: on a poll stream nothing is delivered until the receiver asks, and the two agreeing is a property of push delivery rather than of a healthy transmitter. Sessions counts the DISTINCT sessions this receiver has been told about, across all of its streams together.
sessions.clearNote: Clearing forgets the RECORD. Nobody is signed out and no stream is touched — this page is what has been SAID about these sessions, and a control here that ended one would be a monitoring page with a weapon on it.
appRow.noStreamTip: Declared for Shared Signals and no stream has been agreed. That is the ordinary state of a receiver that has not connected yet, and it is the first thing to check when nothing arrives.
appRow.noStreamTipShort: Declared for Shared Signals and no stream has been agreed.
appRow.sameTip: The receiver asked its Security Event Tokens to be addressed to the same name it authenticated as. That is the ordinary case and not a requirement: `aud` is the receiver's own choice and this service never defaults it.
appRow.noAudTip: No stream, so nothing is addressed anywhere yet.
sessionRow.tip: Everything that has been said about this session, in order
accountRow.tip: Everything that has been said about this account, in order
accountRow.suppressedTip: Events this transmitter built and did NOT send, because the account is in the RISC opt-out state. A count here is the one number on this page that says a receiver heard nothing ON PURPOSE.
accounts.otherNames: {n} account(s) are tracked under other names.
accounts.none1: No accounts are tracked. Change one in the directory — delete a person, set active to false over
accounts.none2: , change a mail address with an ldapmodify — and a row appears here whether or not any stream is agreed, which is what makes “nothing arrived” traceable to “nobody asked”.
accounts.noStreams: No streams. Nothing this service says about an account has anywhere to go, and every row above will show a count of zero however much the directory changes.
accounts.riscOff: RISC is turned off (risc.enabled), so nothing new is being recorded here. What is below is what was recorded before it was turned off.
accounts.autoOff: Automatic emission is off (risc.autoEmit). Accounts still appear here and their state still follows what really happens in the directory, and nothing goes out unless somebody emits it from
accounts.intro: One row per account this service has been told anything about, including accounts that no longer exist. That is deliberate and it is the whole reason this page exists: a purged account is gone from the directory entirely, so a row whose lifecycle is purged is the only remaining evidence that this service ever told anybody it was. The counts are per event type and they never forget; WHICH events those were is
accounts.twoColumns: The lifecycle and the opt-out state are two columns and not one. They move independently: an account can be opted out and perfectly healthy, or compromised and still exchanging. A CAEP session has one state because a session is alive or it is not; an account has three that a receiver acts on differently.
accounts.honourOn: risc.honourOptOut is on, so an account in the opt-out state has its events SUPPRESSED and the Suppressed column counts them — the one number on this page that says a receiver heard nothing on purpose. The four opt-out events themselves are never suppressed: opt-out-effective is an event announcing that there will be no more events, and opt-in is the only way a receiver ever learns the account came back.
accounts.honourOff: risc.honourOptOut is OFF, so events go out about accounts that have opted out of RISC exchange. RISC section 2.8 says an opted-out account is not participating; this is how a receiver that ignores an opt-out gets to be shown doing it.
accounts.heading: Accounts
accounts.drillNote: Every identifier in the first column opens that account on its own page — what has actually been sent about it, in order, with what the register noticed as each one was applied.
accounts.searchPlaceholder: a username, a subject, an email address or a DN
accounts.searchWhat: It matches the account identifier, the sub, the email address, the telephone number, the SSF subject as a receiver was sent it, the directory DN — and every identifier this account has been known by FORMERLY. That last one is not thoroughness: identifier-changed is an event about the key itself, so the address a reader arrives holding is routinely the one the account no longer has.
accounts.perPage: Only the accounts table is paged.
accounts.whereHeading: Where a RISC event could go
accounts.zeroNote: An account with a count of zero almost always means no stream asked for that type rather than anything being wrong. SSF has no refusal for an event type a transmitter will not deliver — its absence from events_delivered is the only notice a receiver gets — so this table is where that shows up.
accounts.perApp: What this transmitter has said to each receiver, across every account. The table above this one is per STREAM and the one above that is per ACCOUNT; this is the third question, and it is the one somebody arrives with once more than one receiver exists.
accounts.receiverWhat: It matches the application name, the identifier it authenticated as, and the aud on its streams. It does NOT match the event types: a receiver that takes none of the fourteen is exactly the row somebody is looking for when they ask why nothing arrived.
accounts.clearNote: Clearing forgets the RECORD. Nobody is disabled, nobody is deleted and no directory entry is touched — this page is what has been SAID about these accounts, and a control here that purged one would be a monitoring page with a weapon on it.
opt.optOut: RISC section 2.8: this account is not participating in event exchange, so nothing but an opt-out event is sent about it while risc.honourOptOut is on.
opt.initiated: The person asked to stop and exchange CARRIES ON for a while. That delay exists to stop a hijacker opting out the moment they take an account over and silencing the events that would report them.
session.notFound: No tracked session is called {id}. That is not necessarily a wrong link. This register is capped at caep.maxSessionsTracked sessions and drops the oldest, and the Clear the register button on the sessions table empties it outright — so an old link coming back empty is the ordinary outcome on a service that has been running a while. What it does NOT mean is that the session was never real: nothing here is ever deleted because a session ended, and a session that ended is exactly what this register is for keeping.
session.name1: Name a session. This page draws ONE of them and the way to it is a link on
session.name2: — every identifier there is one. It is keyed on the session identifier this service gave the session, which is what the SSF subject sent to a receiver names.
session.nothing1: Nothing has been said about this session. That is the ordinary case when no stream asked for the type, and it is the answer to “why did nothing arrive” nine times out of ten —
session.intro: Everything this transmitter has said about one session. The sessions table counts HOW MANY events of each type went out; this says WHICH, in order, with what the register noticed as each one was applied. They are separate on purpose — the state machine and the counters answer different questions, and ssf/caep.ts argues why.
session.heading: The session
saidHeading: What has been said about it
session.warningNote: A warning in the last column is this register's own reading of an event it had just applied — a state change that was not a transition, a payload member the type does not define — and not something a receiver was told. SSF has no channel for that: an event either goes out or does not.
eventsPerPage: It applies to the event list below.
session.perTypeNote: The same eight columns the sessions table carries, written out with room for each type's whole name. A count of zero almost always means no stream asked for that type rather than anything being wrong.
session.resetNote: It forgets what has been SAID about this session and puts its state back to where it started. Nobody is signed out and no stream is touched — a control on a monitoring page that ended a session would be a monitoring page with a weapon on it.
facts.subject: Subject
facts.formerlyTip: An event naming one of these still counts against this row. That is what keeps identifier-changed from splitting one person into two rows at the moment their identifier moves.
account.notFound: No tracked account is called {id}. That is not necessarily a wrong link. This register is capped at risc.maxAccountsTracked accounts and drops the oldest, and the Clear the register button on the accounts table empties it outright. What it does NOT mean is that the account was never real: nothing here is deleted because a person was, and a person who was deleted is exactly what this register is for keeping.
account.name1: Name an account. This page draws ONE of them and the way to it is a link on
account.nothing1: Nothing has been said about this account. That is the ordinary case when no stream asked for the type, and it is the answer to “why did nothing arrive” nine times out of ten —
account.intro: Everything this transmitter has said about one account. The accounts table counts HOW MANY events of each type went out; this says WHICH, in order, with what the register noticed as each one was applied. They are separate on purpose — the state machine and the counters answer different questions, and ssf/risc.ts argues why.
account.heading: The account
account.warningNote: A warning in the last column is this register's own reading of an event it had just applied — a state change that RISC section 2.8's diagram has no arrow for, a payload member the type does not define — and not something a receiver was told. SSF has no channel for that: an event either goes out or does not.
account.perTypeNote: The same fourteen columns the accounts table carries, written out with room for each type's whole name. A count of zero almost always means no stream asked for that type.
account.resetNote: It forgets what has been SAID about this account and puts its state back to where it started — except the holder's opt-out choice, which is theirs (RISC section 2.8) and is kept. The directory entry is untouched — nobody is enabled, disabled or restored, and a control on a monitoring page that did any of those would be a monitoring page with a weapon on it.
